items.title: Iran Unleashed
items.description: For years, Iran confronted a balance of power in the Middle East that tilted against it. The region was dominated by a hostile American superpower, a nuclear-armed and militarily superior Israel, and significant local actors—Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates—that were strategically and economically aligned with the United States. Today finds Iran in entirely new circumstances. It has gone head-to-head with the superpower and Israel, withstood a pounding from their most advanced weapons, and more than survived. As a result, Iran has, with American help, completely reconfigured the power structure of the Middle East and the Persian Gulf. The dominant power in the region going forward will be Iran, not the U.S. or Israel. Neighboring countries are already making their adjustments to this new reality. More distant powers will too. For years, the world has been dealing with an Iran constrained. It will now discover what Iran unleashed looks like. Iran doesn’t need a deal with the United States. The common assumption that a weak and impoverished Iran would eventually have to make some accommodation to American power, open the Strait of Hormuz, and set about tending to its badly damaged economy has proved mistaken. The Islamic Republic has rarely appeared weaker or more vulnerable than it has over the past two years. Last February, President Trump renewed his “maximum pressure” campaign of international sanctions, which severely damaged Iran’s already-weak economy and cut billions of dollars in state revenues. Israel and the United States then launched the 12-day war that June to destroy Iranian nuclear facilities. The war significantly damaged Iran’s program and revealed just how vulnerable the country was to Israeli and American strikes. Then, in February, the United States and Israel launched the most recent war with the killing of the regime’s supreme leader and the great majority of its senior officials, followed by more than five weeks of unremitting attacks on Iranian military capabilities. [ Tom Nichols: Donald Trump effectively just told Iran to get a nuclear weapon ] Yet through all of this, the regime has survived and made no concessions. On the contrary, Iran exposed America’s Achilles’ heel: the vulnerability of Iran’s neighbors. A major turning point came in mid-March, when Israel attacked Iran’s South Pars gas field, and Iran retaliated against Qatar’s Ras Laffan complex, the world’s largest liquefied-natural-gas facility. The attack showed that although Iran obviously could not defeat the United States in an air war, Iranian missiles and drones could inflict enough damage on the oil-and-gas infrastructure of the Gulf to plunge the world into a prolonged economic crisis. The Gulf States understood this immediately, and so did Trump. He halted attacks on Iranian energy targets, ordered a reluctant Israel to do the same, and soon brought the larger campaign to a stop without extracting a single Iranian concession. Ever since, and despite many threats, Trump has not once ordered another strike against Iranian energy infrastructure. This alone was enough to alter the balance of leverage between Iran and the United States. From April through last month, Trump repeatedly threatened to launch another massive attack against Iran. Each time, Iran threatened retaliation, Gulf States warned of the consequences, and Trump backed off. By his third or fourth bluff, Tehran had reason to conclude that the United States was no longer prepared to follow Iran up the ladder of escalation. Trump made this clear when he noted in mid-June that continuing the war would lead to “economic catastrophe,” possibly even a “depression,” and that he did not want to become President Herbert Hoover. Ever since, Trump has been trying, with notable desperation, to end the conflict. The memorandum of understanding that the U.S. and Iran adopted in June reflected this reality. Although phrased to save face for the United States as much as possible, the MOU was a clear Iranian victory. It declared that the Islamic Republic of Iran, and no other nation, would “make arrangements” for the “safe passage of commercial vessels” through the Strait of Hormuz. In dialogue with Oman, without intermediaries or other participants, Iran would determine the strait’s administration “in line with the applicable international law and the sovereign rights of coastal states.” The MOU did not call for a return to the prewar status quo. Neither did it provide the United States any say over future administration of the strait. Rather, it designated Iran as the only actor other than the weak Oman, and it even allowed Iran to charge nations for safe passage after 60 days. The MOU thus codified the defeat that the United States had suffered back in March, when Trump apparently realized that he either could not or would not risk further attacks on energy facilities in the region. In retrospect, Iran’s leaders do not seem to have believed that they needed the MOU. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei reportedly had to be persuaded by President Masoud Pezeshkian to sign it. Tehran’s relative indifference was understandable: The American concessions reflected such desperation to end the war that the Iranians could well have expected that the U.S. would eventually retreat, with or without a deal. Iranian leaders certainly did not hesitate to blow up the cease-fire almost immediately when the U.S. Navy began shepherding tankers through the Omani side of the strait. Trump may or may not have understood the full extent of the concessions his negotiators had made regarding control of the strait, but from the Iranian point of view, the Omani route was an attempt to recapture what the U.S. had given away. For a while, the United States and Iran engaged in tit-for-tat strikes, culminating in intense American attacks in mid-July. When these had no effect, Trump warned on July 15 that the United States was “going to knock out all their power plants” and “all their bridges” unless Iran negotiated. Yet again, no attack followed. Then the world, and the Iranians, learned one of the main reasons: Revelations that American stocks of crucial munitions were dangerously low, and that no less than the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff himself was looking for an “off-ramp,” sent a clear signal about the future course of American strategy. A major assault on Iran would threaten American interests elsewhere by weakening the United States in the possible event of a Chinese move on Taiwan or a Russian onslaught against a NATO member. Missile shortages would also increase the hazards involved in a massive attack on Iranian infrastructure. The U.S. would be forced to send more manned aircraft within range of Iranian air defenses, and it would have relatively few interceptors on hand to protect the Gulf States and its own regional bases. The risk of American casualties would be high, as would the danger to the region’s energy infrastructure. And nothing would guarantee that such an assault would be any more effective than the five-plus weeks of bombings were earlier this year. American actions have made plain that Washington fears escalation more than Iran does—not just for now, but for the future. This places limits on what the United States can do even at low levels of conflict. Because any military action against Iran risks stepping onto an escalation ladder that the U.S. does not want to ascend, even tit-for-tat strikes seem no longer to be part of American strategy. The president has reportedly told his advisers that he does not want to order more strikes. The Iranians have struck at several UAE ships this month and even fired ballistic missiles at the country, but the United States has not responded since July—a fact undoubtedly noted by the UAE and Iran’s other neighbors. [ Vivian Salama: From ‘indispensable’ ally to target of annihilation ] Given the evident American reluctance to fight another major campaign, Iran has reason to wonder what it can get from a deal that it will not get anyway without one. Senior Iranian officials are now calling for the withdrawal of American forces, the lifting of the American naval blockade and all sanctions, the freeing of Iran’s frozen assets, and the payment of war reparations. The conventional wisdom is that Iran’s leaders know that these demands are nonstarters for Washington and that they are therefore either rubbing Trump’s nose in defeat, angling for a better deal, or overplaying their hand. Many observers still assume that control of the strait is a bargaining chip to squeeze more concessions out of the United States or get Trump back to the MOU. But we are well past all that. A victor does not have to go back to the bargaining table except to set the terms of surrender. Iran has now laid out those terms. They may appear maximalist and excessive, but Tehran must hardly believe that it has reason to ask for less. Iran has made clear for months that control of the strait is not negotiable. The notion, constantly floated by the Trump administration and the media, that the Iranians can’t make up their minds and that they keep shifting their positions is nonsense. As far back as April, Mojtaba declared that Iran would implement “new legal frameworks and management” of the strait and that “foreigners who come from thousands of kilometers away” had no place in the Gulf, “except at the bottom of its waters.” On a day commemorating Iran’s defeat of Portugal in the strait in 1622, he declared that “by the will and power of God, the bright future of the Persian Gulf region will be a future without America.” The idea that, having survived both military strikes and sanctions, Iran will now succumb to sanctions alone is deluded. Mojtaba has overhauled Iran’s national-security leadership and installed veterans of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in top positions. Former IRGC Commander Mohsen Rezaei now heads the Supreme National Security Council, and other hard-line security officials have been elevated. The regime emerging from the war is being reorganized by men who believe that Iran survived an American-Israeli attempt to destroy it and that defiance, not compromise, produced victory. But this is not just triumphalism. For Iran, control of the strait is neither a luxury nor a bargaining chip. Given the likelihood that, at some future point, Israel or the United States will attack again, deal or no deal, the strait provides Iran’s strongest and surest deterrent. It is also the key to unlocking many of the shackles that a U.S.-dominated world order placed on Iran over the course of decades, and to undoing a regional and global economic system designed to exclude and impoverish it. Some so-called moderates within the Iranian establishment may well regard the strait as a bargaining chip, but they are not winning the argument, for reasons that are not hard to understand. An IRGC spokesperson stated the regime’s perspective plainly: “For us, the Strait of Hormuz is not merely an economic waterway, but rather a key component of our geopolitical and strategic power.” Iran has been establishing the mechanisms of control for months and instructing shipowners and nations as to how the system will operate. It created the Persian Gulf Strait Authority and demanded that shipping companies register with it, obtain permits, follow Iran-designated routes, and pay for Iran-provided insurance and security. Neither is Iran claiming merely the right to collect money. It is also claiming the right to decide who may pass. It has proposed excluding vessels associated with governments it deems hostile, such as the U.S. and Israel, and it has demanded compensation from nations that participated in attacks against it. Iran is establishing the principle that passage through the strait will henceforth be a privilege that Tehran can grant, condition, delay, or deny. Other nations have already begun acquiescing to the new arrangement. India, Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, China, and others have sought to come to terms. Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz is a more useful instrument of power than a nuclear weapon would be. A nuclear weapon might deter an attack, but control of the strait gives Iran leverage every day, over dozens of countries. With it, Iran can reward friends, punish enemies, extract revenue, force the loosening of sanctions, and make governments think twice before opposing Iranian policies. It can do all of this without firing a shot, and while preserving the ability to threaten violence when necessary. The sanctions strategy that for decades served to isolate Iran rested on international cooperation. Nations that depend on access to the strait—Japan and South Korea, for example—will have to choose between access to a reliable energy supply and participation in American-backed sanctions. Will they choose solidarity with Washington—this Washington—over their economic interests? In the new order that Iran is creating, a global sanctions regime is likely to be unsustainable. Iran will probably sustain its control over energy flows for at least a couple of years. The most optimistic projections suggest that establishing alternative pipelines and export routes that circumvent the Strait of Hormuz will take this long. But one wonders whether these will even come to fruition. New pipelines, ports, and energy facilities will be just as vulnerable to Iranian missiles and drones as the old ones were. Will Iran simply stand by while neighboring states construct the means to escape its control? The small states that must build and protect such routes are going to be wary of incurring Iran’s wrath, and American protection has proved inadequate. Iran is already trying to draw Iraq away from developing alternative oil-export corridors, in part by offering safe passage for Iraqi tankers on Iranian terms. The regional adjustment has begun . Gulf rulers who once counted on an American security guarantee must now make their peace with the power that proved capable of defeating their protector. Saudi Arabia’s rejection of the U.S.- and Israel-backed Abraham Accords in favor of a strategic compact with Pakistan and Turkey hints at the shape of the future. The Abraham Accords represented the consolidation of Israeli power and influence in the region and the further containment of Iran. The Mecca pact is something else entirely. Neither Pakistan nor Turkey regards Iran as a major threat; Pakistan, like Iran, has close relations with China; Israel regards Turkey as a regional threat second only to Iran. Instead of an American-Israeli order, this will be an alignment less implacably hostile to Iran, less friendly to Israel, and more independent of the United States. The signatories also have nuclear weapons in common: Pakistan has them, and the Turks and Saudis want them. [ Arash Azizi: Tehran has to make a choice ] Meanwhile, Iran will be free to resume its own nuclear-weapons program without fear of another major attack. This fact in itself will transform the regional balance. Last year, Israel and the United States bombed Iran’s nuclear facilities for 12 days without facing serious Iranian retaliation. Now Iran has been emboldened to use its control of the strait, and threats against neighboring states and their energy infrastructure, to deter any such strikes for the foreseeable future. American missile and interceptor stocks will take a long time to replenish, and may well be needed in other parts of the world in years to come; Iran will all the while be rearming with Russian and Chinese help, potentially leaving the U.S. in a worse position a year from now than it is in today. The effects will extend far beyond the Middle East. American allies in Asia and Europe can see that a relatively brief war against a second-rank power has consumed much of America’s supply of the weapons needed for missile defense. They can see that the United States began a war it could not finish, exposed its partners to retaliation, and then stopped when the costs became too great. Beijing’s conclusions about Taiwan, and Moscow’s conclusions about Europe, may be impossible to know. But America’s allies will inevitably be asking whether Washington has the weapons, stamina, and political will to sustain another major conflict. In fact, they already are . That the Iranian regime could fall is, of course, possible. It is corrupt, repressive, economically incompetent, and widely hated by its people. But it had all of these weaknesses before the war. What it did not have was control of the world’s most important energy choke point, the prospect of growing revenues and influence, the demonstrated ability to deter the United States, and the prestige of an impossible victory. A regime that survived what much of the world believed would destroy it, and then forced the world’s dominant power to retreat, will likely emerge strengthened, at least for a time. Such success tends to breed confidence, and perhaps overconfidence. But it is not likely to make Iran’s leaders less ambitious or less committed to the faith that saw them through this miraculous triumph. Recently, senior Iranian officials began talking publicly about adopting a “fully offensive” posture, and reports have emerged of Iranian plans to expand its targets to include European countries hosting American bases. To see stories in The New York Times asking , “Who will blink first?” is amusing, given that the Iranians until now have never once blinked, while the Trump administration has done nothing but blink. Iran may even start fighting again to force the U.S. to lift the naval blockade. Given the American administration’s proven fear of escalation, the hope is not unreasonable. The world has spent decades worrying about what Iran might do if it acquired a nuclear weapon. It should now worry about something even more consequential: an Iran that has defeated the United States, no longer fears American attack, and controls access to the Persian Gulf. Nuclear weapons alone could never have given Iran this kind of power. The failed U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has.

items.title: The Hatred That Broke American Politics
items.description: “If you want to defend the South and Western civilization from the Jew and his dark-skinned allies, be at Charlottesville on 12 August.” Nine years ago, that message spread across the internet. The call was answered by several hundred white supremacists, who marched through the University of Virginia. The rage-filled men carried torches, chanting, “Jews will not replace us.” They swarmed around the historic rotunda, arriving at a statue of the school’s founder, Thomas Jefferson. There they met a tiny band of student counterprotesters who responded with their own chant: “Black lives matter.” That evening turned violent, the first act in a deadly weekend. Most Americans remember the torches, the rage, the death. But those clashing chants also revealed a gap between the targets of hatred and the words available to name it. Race is the wound America sees. Anti-Semitism is the one it doesn’t. Jews have frequently been imagined as a colorless minority whose great persecution took place elsewhere, or as a group whose Christian-adjacent faith flourished with the religious freedom they found in the United States. But their in-betweenness has always been part of the danger: Jews have never fit neatly into America’s frameworks of identity, and that failure to fit has marked them as suspect, out of place, or impossible to categorize. Depending on the audience, Jews are dismissed as beneficiaries of white privilege or treated as not quite white at all—too assimilated and not assimilated enough, too powerful and too marginal. That ambiguity has placed them, again and again, at the center of America’s battles over free speech and equal protection. When hatred does not fit existing categories, we tend either to ignore it or to overcorrect—both responses that distort the boundaries of free expression. Our failure to reckon with the anti-Semitism of Charlottesville—on the right and the left—was not merely a missed opportunity. It helped create the opening into which illiberalism has since rushed. [ David Frum: Anti-Semitism is becoming mainstream ] August 2017 marked a turning point, not just for racial populism but for American democracy. That crisis seeded a surge in anti-Semitism. It also helped produce a government campaign against such bigotry that has become a tool for undermining freedom, championed by the Trump administration only when it serves the White House’s purposes. Meanwhile, the progressive left has struggled to sustain its critique of Israel’s war with Palestine—and of American responsibility for a moral catastrophe—without letting that critique curdle into conspiracism. Americans appear to face an impossible choice between protecting free speech and safeguarding equal rights. But that is a false dichotomy. Honoring both will, however, require de-exceptionalizing anti-Semitism. And that, in turn, necessitates returning to Charlottesville, and reckoning with how both the left and the right failed in its aftermath. Over the course of 2017 , three separate racist rallies took place in Charlottesville. In May, the alt-right provocateur Richard Spencer led a small rally in downtown Charlottesville to protest a city-council decision to remove two century-old Confederate monuments. A University of Virginia alum with a passion for Wagnerian opera, Spencer dressed old hatred in new clothes. He spoke grandly of restoring white supremacy, and of defeating liberal conspiracies to change America beyond recognition. President Trump’s election gave him cause for hope that Black Lives Matter and antifa would be crushed. “We will not be replaced from this world,” Spencer screamed as plumes of green and gray smoke from flares rose into the sky. “Whites have a future! We have a future of power!” Two months later, the Ku Klux Klan paraded through town. Although they had come to protest the removal of a statue of Robert E. Lee, they held banners denouncing Jewish communism and the satanic Talmud. They were met with a massive, raucous counterprotest, inspired in part by a newly formed Black Lives Matter chapter in town, staged by citizens determined to oppose the hatred. This article was adapted from James Loeffler’s forthcoming book, Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and the Fight over Free Speech in Modern America n August brought round three: Spencer returned to town, accompanied by a who’s who of the far right, answering the call to join what they labeled the “Battle of Charlottesville.” Officially, Unite the Right was a free-speech march in defense of the monument. But several organizers had ties to violent extremist groups and online they made their intentions clear. “Next stop: Charlottesville, VA. Final stop: Auschwitz,” wrote Andrew Anglin of The Daily Stormer . The planners fantasized about mowing down protesters with cars, and repeating the Holocaust—even as they denied it happened. They wrapped retrograde hatred in constitutional pretense. Free speech became both shield and sword. The weekend brought mayhem: dozens of injuries, the murder of Heather Heyer, the death of two state troopers. Yet it also exposed the entanglement of race and religion in the racist imagination, which conceived of Jews as invisible power brokers, racial chameleons, white imposters, and anti-Christian infidels. Charlottesville shocked the country. Yet in its aftermath, America had no vocabulary for describing anti-Semitism in relation to other hatreds—let alone for responding to it. Then–UVA President Teresa Sullivan denounced the violence and “racist, anti-immigrant, homophobic and misogynistic chants,” but made no mention of Jews. The great majority of other statements issued by Virginia-college presidents repeated the same failure. The local school superintendent discarded her back-to-school speech and instead spoke of the need to name “the hate that had visited our city,” which had targeted “our Latino, Muslim, bisexual, transgender, Christian, and Black students.” Jews, again, went unmentioned. These educators were not anti-Semites. They were well-meaning liberals for whom other forms of hatred eclipsed anti-Semitism; anti-Black racism, for one, loomed larger. But anti-Semitism was hardly new to Charlottesville. The poet Karl Shapiro wrote of his time at UVA in the 1930s: “To hurt the Negro and avoid the Jew is the curriculum.” The dean once tracked applicants in three categories: “Virginians, non-Virginians, and Hebrews.” And that was not true of just Virginia. Americans have long been accustomed to seeing Jews as a model minority whose success proved their belonging, and to dismissing anti-Jewish hatred as something that happened elsewhere. Without having reckoned with their nation’s own long history of anti-Semitism, Americans met it in 2017 with confusion and silence. The centrist liberal response constituted a form of occlusion. White supremacy was understood strictly in racial terms, and anti-Semitism was blocked from view. The chants in Charlottesville fixated on Jews. The response did not. What liberals failed to see, the populist right first denied, then exploited. Trump could not condemn the marchers without asserting there were “very fine people on both sides.” For two years, his administration shrugged off any serious response. Then the strategy shifted. Trump seized on anti-Semitism—but only anti-Semitism from the left. A 2019 executive order focused on college campuses, targeting anti-Zionist expression while lifting anti-Semitism out of the broader landscape of hatred for special treatment. This marked the first moment in which Trump threatened to defund American universities without even a proper investigation. Anti-Semitism became a cudgel for the administration to wield against political enemies and liberal institutions, not a hatred to be fought on equal, consistent terms. The same pattern played out in Virginia. Glenn Youngkin tried to ignore Charlottesville entirely while running for governor in 2021. On his first day in office, he issued several executive orders. One of them banned “inherently divisive concepts” such as critical race theory from classrooms in the name of free speech. Another announced a commission on anti-Semitism whose final report reduced Charlottesville to two paragraphs out of 13,000 words. Many Republican politicians chose to attack civil-rights protections for most minorities while selectively championing them in the Jewish case. Genuine anti-Semitism was met with a sledgehammer instead of a scalpel, violating other rights in the process. UVA faced a wholesale attack as part of the wave of disproportionate punishments inflicted on institutions of higher education in the aftermath of October 7, 2023. But the institution’s vulnerability had deeper roots. The progressive left had its own failure to reckon with—one that played out on campus and left universities unable to articulate a coherent defense when the attacks came. The progressive left failed by exclusion. After the weekend of terror in 2017, UVA’s Jewish Leadership Council worked with the Minority Rights Coalition on repair and renewal. Yet when they applied to join as a member organization, they were rejected on account of their pro-Israel affiliate group. Remove that Zionist organization, they were told, and they could join. After objections that Jews had been prime victims, a compromise was floated: Jewish students could join as an honorary minority group without voting rights. Jewish student leaders, among them a young woman who had fled fearing her life on August 11, denounced the moral myopia. As this conflict escalated in spring 2018, pro-Palestinian protesters stormed a Hillel event featuring Israeli Druze and Jewish reserve soldiers. Shouting slogans through a megaphone, they denounced Zionists as fascists and refused “dialogue with racists.” Their heckler’s veto muddled their critique of Israeli military propaganda. Jewish students claimed the rhetoric threatened them; protesters said the soldiers’ presence did the same to Palestinian students. Everyone claimed the mantle of free speech while denouncing the other side as perpetrators of hate speech. The progressive left, for all of its commitment to confronting hatred, rarely turned that lens inward. The question of where anti-Zionism ended and anti-Semitism began was dismissed, not deliberated. That moment was a rehearsal for every debate we’ve lived through since. How do you balance free speech and equal rights when competing groups on campus have political and personal ties to a live conflict? Where does legitimate critique end and hatred begin? All of it was there, seven years ago, before October 7, before the campus protests of 2024. When war erupted again, Americans were unprepared. Each side had made its cause exceptional—anti-Semitism a unique hatred, Zionism a unique evil—and that rhetorical brinksmanship left no room for the harder work of ensuring uniform equality and pluralism for all. From silence to chaos, we found ourselves without a coherent language to combat hatred. The past several years have illustrated an old Yiddish saying: Lekh mikh nisht, un lakh mikh nisht . Literally: “Don’t beat me, and don’t lick me.” But in effect: Don’t demonize us, but don’t fetishize us, either. Since Charlottesville, Jews have been both demonized and tokenized across the political spectrum. Building a way forward requires de-exceptionalizing anti-Semitism—not erasing its distinct features, but treating it as one hatred among others, deserving the same protections, no more and no less. [ Yair Rosenberg: The anti-Semitic revolution on the American right ] This wisdom extends beyond Jews. Every group deserves protection from hatred without becoming a political football. Every group deserves to be seen clearly—neither as villain nor as mascot. That includes Palestinian Americans, who have watched their own dehumanization dismissed while anti-Semitism is used against their speech. This is why we need a new model—one that treats no group’s claim to protection as special, one that recognizes free speech and equal protection as complementary values enabling all citizens to participate fully in democratic life. Building that model will require Jewish communal leaders to resist the politicization of Jewish fear—and progressive coalitions to make room for Jewish particularity without imposing a litmus test on Jews alone. What would this look like in practice? Rejecting the warping of anti-Semitism for partisan ends. Acknowledging anti-Semitism from all directions rather than only the versions that serve our politics. Building democratic coalitions across differences rather than demanding ideological purity as the price of admission. Nine years after Charlottesville, we have seen the stumbles and overcorrections, the cynicism and despair. What we haven’t done is imagine a better future in which fighting anti-Semitism strengthens civil rights for all. That work begins with honesty about how we got here. The bigots who marched in Charlottesville were real. So is our capacity to build something better. In 2017, two chants collided in the dark. We can still answer them together. This article was adapted from James Loeffler’s forthcoming book, Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and the Fight over Free Speech in Modern America

items.title: Spantik Peak mission to retrieve body of Pakistani climber halted amid heavy snowfall
items.description: GILGIT: Snowfall at Spantik Peak on Sunday halted efforts to retrieve the body of Pakistani climber Dr Asma Mushtaq, who died while descending the 7,027m peak in Gilgit-Baltistan’s Shigar district. 34-year-old Dr Mushtaq died at an altitude of around 6,250 metres on Thursday while descending from the summit of Spantik — also known as Golden Peak — after suffering from high-altitude sickness. Her body is currently at Camp 3. High-altitude sickness encompasses a range of pulmonary and cerebral conditions caused by hypoxia, or oxygen deprivation, due to rapid ascent and inadequate acclimatisation to high altitudes. Baltistan Division Commissioner Kamal Khan told Dawn that the rescue team of six high-altitude porters had reached Camp 2 and had attempted to start their mission towards Camp 3, but were forced to retreat back to Base Camp due to heavy rain and snow. “Due to continuous heavy snowfall and extremely strong winds, conditions have become very dangerous and risky,” he said. “The rescue team could not safely remain at Camp 2, therefore, the entire rescue team had to turn back.” He said that the team had now reached Base Camp safely and that further rescue efforts would be considered when the weather conditions improved. “The mission is being undertaken under extremely challenging high-altitude and weather conditions, and the safety of the recovery team remains a priority,” he said. According to a press release issued by the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) General Secretary Ayaz Shigri on Saturday, Dr Mushtaq’s body remains at approximately 6,400m. “The recovery team departed yesterday (i.e. Friday) and reached Camp 2 today (Saturday), but operations have been halted due to heavy snowfall,” the statement said. “The team has been advised to return to Base Camp and wait for a suitable weather window.” Approval for a mercy mission for helicopter rescue on humanitarian grounds was also in progress, with the support of the Pakistan Army, it added. The ACP statement noted that the recovery operation, consisting of climbers from different teams, was being coordinated by Dr Mushtaq’s own expedition company, in coordination with institutions including the tourism department, local government and ACP. “It was earlier reported that Dr Asma suffered from high-altitude sickness after summiting,” the press release said. “The circumstances surrounding her death, as well as the conduct and response of the expedition company, will be fully investigated once the teams are safely down and her body has been recovered.” Any necessary action would follow the findings of that investigation, it added. View this post on Instagram It also clarified ACP’s role in the venture, stating that the club was Pakistan’s national federation for mountaineering and sport climbing and not a rescue organisation with dedicated resources. Search, rescue and other relevant activities depended upon government resources, it noted, while regretting that Pakistan currently lacked a dedicated and properly established high-altitude rescue system. The ACP said that under the new leadership of the club, it was working with the relevant authorities to help with the development of an effective rescue framework and support improvements to the country’s mountaineering infrastructure. “Please refrain from spreading misinformation or making unverified claims about the recovery operation,” the club requested, noting that the safe and dignified recovery of Dr Mushtaq’s body was the priority. Shigri told Dawn that misinformation was being spread about the delay in the recovery of the body. He said that efforts were being made to recover the body from the peak and transport it to the base camp so that it could be airlifted via helicopter, pointing out that helicopters could not retrieve the body from altitudes over 6,000m. “Only the ground rescue team can bring down the body from the peak to base camp,” he said, noting that a six-member local team was making efforts in this regard. “Initially, certain confusions arose regarding the remuneration demanded by the high-altitude porters for undertaking the body recovery operation, which resulted in a delay in commencement of the recovery mission,” Khan told Dawn . According to the commissioner, no agreement had been signed between the tour operator and the mountaineer, and no insurance had been arranged for helicopter evacuation. The matter was subsequently taken up through the joint intervention and coordination of the Baltistan division civil administration, the tourism department, the GB government, EV-K2-CNR — an Italian NGO paying the expenses of the ground rescue team — and the ACP, he said. “Through their coordinated efforts, the matter was amicably resolved, and the required arrangements were finalised,” he added. Earlier, the commissioner had told Dawn that the tour operator had violated mountaineering rules by not arranging for the recovery team to retrieve Dr Mushtaq’s body from Spantik Peak and for helicopters to airlift the body from base camp to Skardu. “Under the rules, if a ground rescue team or helicopter is needed, the tour operator is responsible to arrange a rescue team and pay insurance for helicopter,” he said. The commissioner added that the operator had not conducted a briefing or debriefing either, which he said was mandatory under the Mountaineering Rules 1999. However, Khan rejected the “wrongful” impression that the recovery mission was delayed by the operator’s negligence, noting that the division and district administrations had arranged the ground team soon after the incident with an NGO paying the expenses. The Pakistan Army also agreed to provide a helicopter to airlift the body from the base camp to Skardu on humanitarian grounds. He said the mission depended on the weather: “If the weather allows, the rescue team will bring the body down to base camp, and army helicopters will airlift it from the base camp to Skardu.” Experts say bringing a body down from a high-altitude peak, particularly from above 6,000m, is an extremely risky and challenging task. In many cases, bodies at such extreme altitudes are left and buried under the snow rather than being brought down. Sajid Sadpara buried the body of his father, renowned Pakistani mountaineer Ali Sadpara , at around 8,000m on K2 in 2021. GB tourism department officials requested that people consider the risks and circumstances carefully before making comments about Dr Mushtaq’s case. Information Minister Ataullah Tarar also shared the update on his X account. He further stated, “Heli has been authorised and coordination has been done between [the] GB government and Force Commander Northern Areas. Alternate arrangements are also in place. Whatever can be done in these circumstances will be done,” he wrote, adding that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was being “kept updated on the situation. According to her social media profiles, Mushtaq was originally from Lahore and worked as a UK-based doctor specialising in obstetrics and gynaecology. Away from her medical profession, she was a passionate traveller, vlogger and mountaineer who actively documented her expeditions on social media. She completed a successful winter ascent of the 4,076-metre Musa ka Musallah peak and was associated with expeditions to Rupal and Arandu. In a 2024 post seeking K2 sponsorship, she described herself as “a doctor and mountaineer”. Broad Peak operation remains halted amid bad weather Meanwhile, due to continued bad weather conditions, helicopters were unable to fly to Broad Peak to airlift the body of US climber Sarah Mallory Geis from the base camp after the deadly avalanche that killed a 10-member expedition. The body of US climber was recovered by three local porters voluntarily from Broad Peak (8,047m) on Friday, 22 days after she went missing in a deadly avalanche . Local volunteers have moved the body to Broad Peak basecamp. Shigri said that as the weather improved, the body of the US climber would be airlifted to Skardu via Pakistan Army helicopters. Geis was among the 10 members of an expedition that went missing on July 30 after a deadly avalanche on Broad Peak. The avalanche struck on July 30, cutting off contact with the international expedition led by world-renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja on Broad Peak, one of the world’s highest mountains. Purja’s company later confirmed there were no survivors . Shigri said that nine of the climbers, including Purja and Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi , had so far been recovered and handed over to families. He added that the search for the tenth deceased member, Nawang Thindu Sherpa, would continue. Broad Peak is the world’s 12th highest mountain, located in the Karakoram range, and is regarded as one of the toughest and most technical climbs of all the 8,000-metre-plus ascents. It was first summited in 1957 by an Austrian team.

items.title: Deux voix, une même aube : la naissance du Prophète chez Al-Busîrî et Cheikh El Hadji Malick Sy
items.description: Durant la 4e nuit de récital de la Burdah à Tivaouane, tel qu’institué par Cheikh El Hadji Malick Sy, c’est le chapitre intitulé « De sa Nativité » qui est chanté et médité. Sept siècles et deux continents séparent l'Égypte mamelouke d'Al-Busîrî (VIIe/XIIIe siècle) du Sénégal de Cheikh El Hadji Malick Sy (XIXe-XXe siècle). Pourtant, les deux hommes, deux grands poètes mystiques se retrouvent sur un même terrain : celui du madîh nabawî, l'éloge poétique du Prophète Muhammad, et plus précisément celui des irhâsât. Ce sont les signes annonciateurs et prodiges qui, selon la tradition, ont accompagné la naissance de l’Élu. En comparant le passage de la Burda d'Al-Busîrî consacré à cette nuit et le chapitre que Cheikh Malick Sy lui consacre dans son Khilâçu Dhahab fî Sîrat Khayr al-'Arab (« L’Or décanté, sur la biographie du meilleur des Arabes »), on voit se dessiner deux manières, apparentées mais distinctes, de raconter le même événement fondateur. Al-Busîrî : la nuit où l’empire perse vacille Le passage extrait du chapitre de la Burda consacré à la naissance et à la mission prophétique, construit son émerveillement autour d'un décor très précis : la cour de Perse. Le palais de Kisrâ (Chosroès) se fissure « comme se disperse une assemblée sans jamais se ressouder » ; le feu sacré des zoroastriens, entretenu depuis des siècles, s'éteint « de chagrin » ; le lac de Sâwa se retire et refuse ses eaux à qui vient y boire. Busîrî pousse l'image jusqu'au paradoxe : le feu, dit-il, porte en lui l'humidité propre à l'eau tant il est accablé de tristesse, et l'eau porte l'ardeur propre au feu. À cette scène de désolation s'ajoutent les djinns qui poussent des cris, les augures et les devins qui perdent leur don, les idoles qui s'effondrent, les étoiles filantes qui repoussent les démons voulant surprendre la révélation. Les vaincus fuyant « comme les héros d'Abraha », ou comme les cailloux incandescents lancés par les oiseaux sur l’armée de celui qui voulait détruire la Ka’bah. Là, Busîrî se rapproche plus de Cheikh El Hadji Malick dans une autre de ses odes la Nûniyya. Mais, ce que fait Busîrî ici relève d'un style rhétorique précise : il ancre la naissance du Prophète dans une géopolitique religieuse. La Perse sassanide, rivale de Byzance et gardienne du zoroastrisme, est le symbole même de la puissance « païenne » préislamique. En la faisant vaciller au moment même de la naissance, Busîrî transforme un événement qui semblait isolé – la naissance d'un enfant à La Mecque – en un basculement de l'histoire universelle. Le ton est presque taquin et ironique : « ils sont devenus aveugles et sourds » (v. 8), dit-il des Perses, qui n'ont ni entendu l'annonce ni vu l'éclair de l'avertissement, alors même que leur propre devin les avait prévenus que leur religion tordue ne tiendrait pas. Cheikh Malick Sy : une nuit où tout l'univers se met en mouvement Le chapitre correspondant du Khilâçu Dhahab un vaste poème didactique de plusieurs centaines de vers, organisé en fusûl (chapitres) numérotés, signe d'un texte pensé pour l'enseignement autant que pour la dévotion, reprend le même fonds narratif des irhâsât, choses et évènements sortant de l’ordinaire, mais en élargit considérablement le registre. On y trouve d'abord la même représentation que chez Busîrî : « Quelle nuit resplendissante ! », « le trône de tout roi fut retourné, sans exception. Par le Seigneur de la Kaaba sacrée ». Mais là où Busîrî nommait un empire précis, Cheikh El Hadji Malick Sy universalise le motif : ce n'est plus seulement Kisrâ qui vacille, c'est tout roi, toute idole, (Sarîru kulli malîkin) ; c’est humanité entière qui est saisie par l'événement. Nous l’évoquions dans Inspirations Malickiennes, « là où Seydi El Hadji Malick Sy innove c’est dans sa connaissance du contexte socio-historique dans lequel vécut le Prophète. Il navigue, constamment, entre la vie du Prophète et l’évocation de ce contexte avec une culture historique qui peut étonner plus d’un. Malgré le manque chronique d’ouvrages de références qui caractérisa son époque, la difficulté de les acquérir, sans parler de la complexité de l’environnement historique qui vit la naissance du Prophète (PSL), Maodo nous abreuve de connaissances sur Rome, Byzance, Chosroes, Anou Shirwân et les autres. Sa connaissance géographique doublée de sa maitrise de l’histoire qui se dégage de nombreux écrits reste encore une énigme et une source d’admiration pour quelqu’un qui n’a quitté le Sénégal que pour le pèlerinage à la Mecque. Lorsque Seydi El Hadji Malick Sy, dans son approche de la vie du Prophète et du berceau de la révélation, le Hedjaz, en arrive à donner, avec une précision inouïe, les noms de lieux et de repères encore méconnus par les habitants-mêmes de ces régions, l’on ne peut qu’encore admirer ses efforts inestimables pour l’acquisition du savoir » Convergences et divergences : deux théologies de l'émerveillement Les deux poètes puisent manifestement dans le même réservoir de traditions de la Sîra (Ibn Ishâq, Tabarî, et la littérature ultérieure des dalâ'il al-nubuwwa, les « preuves de la prophétie ») : chute des idoles, renversement des trônes, agitation des djinns, signes dans le ciel. Il est d'ailleurs très probable que Cheikh Malick Sy, en fin lettré, héritier de la tradition Tijaniyya où la Burda est mémorisée et récitée depuis des siècles, ait délibérément fait résonner son propre texte avec celui de Busîrî dont il partage la rime « m » d’où la Mîmiyya. La possibilité est aussi grande qu’un tel procédé s’agisse d’intertextualité qui fait dialoguer les textes de diverses manières, mais reflétant le partage d’une même tradition poétique bien ancrée. Mais, c’est, surtout, l'accent qui diffère : ● Busîrî construit une scène à dominante politique et polémique : c'est la chute d'un empire rival, la Perse zoroastrienne, qui incarne l'aveuglement du monde pré-islamique. Le registre est celui de la disgrâce et de l'humiliation d'une puissance identifiable. ● Cheikh El Hadji Malick Sy construit une scène à dominante cosmologique et sapientielle : l'univers entier avec les animaux, les mers, les cieux, les femmes saintes du passé, les anges, jusqu'au nourrisson lui-même. Tout participe à l'accueil du Prophète et de cette nativité fondatrice. Chez Maodo, le cadre est moins celui d'un empire humilié que celui d'une harmonie universelle qui se réorganise autour de la Lumière muhammadienne, doctrine que Cheikh El Hadji Malick Sy pose d'ailleurs dès le premier chapitre de son œuvre, consacré à l'origine préexistante de cette lumière avant même la généalogie du Prophète signature typiquement soufie de sa démarche. Cet aspcet est largement mis en évidence dans les travaux de Seydi Diamil Niane de l’IFAN. Sur le plan formel, les deux textes partagent la forme classique de la qasîda à rime unique filée sur des dizaines, voire des centaines de vers. Mais leur destination diffère : la Burda circule avant tout comme texte dévotionnel et mystique, récité pour la baraka et la guérison (Busîrî l'aurait composée après une guérison miraculeuse) ; le Khilâçu Dhahab, de Cheikh El Hadji Malick Sy se présente comme une sîra versifiée complète, structurée en chapitres numérotés et annotée philologiquement une sorte de manuel destiné aux apprenant de tous siècles autant qu'un poème de louange. La naissance du Prophète continue d'être racontée dans deux poèmes que séparent plusieurs siècles, mais chaque poète y projette l'univers qui est le sien : Busîrî y voit l'effondrement d'un empire rival et la victoire du vrai sur le faux ; Cheikh El Hadji Malick Sy y voit la mise en branle de la création entière, des profondeurs marines jusqu'aux cieux, autour de la Lumière qui, en lui, a toujours précédé le monde. Les deux textes, loin de se concurrencer ou se contredire, interagissent et se répondent : ils montrent la vitalité d'une même tradition de louange prophétique qui, du Nil au fleuve Sénégal, n'a cessé de se réinventer sans jamais quitter son fonds commun. Dr. Bakary SAMBE, Centre d’étude des religions, Université Gaston Berger de Saint-Louis (Sénégal)

items.title: Éboulement de Dar-es-Salam : plusieurs victimes ensevelies, des familles à la recherche de leurs proches
items.description: Quelques années après un premier éboulement meurtrier à la décharge de Dar-es-Salam, une nouvelle catastrophe s’est produite dans la nuit de samedi à dimanche dans cette zone de Conakry. Une importante masse d’ordures a cédé tard dans la nuit et s’est abattue sur des habitations situées à proximité de la décharge, dans le secteur Radars.Selon des témoins, plusieurs personnes seraient encore ensevelies sous les décombres. Le bilan humain reste, pour l’heure, inconnu, mais cette nouvelle catastrophe aurait fait plusieurs victimes. Un immeuble de type R+2, qui servait notamment d’habitation, s’est affaissé sous l’effet de l’éboulement. Les opérations de secours et de dégagement se poursuivent sur place, avec la mobilisation d’engins et de machines. Le Premier ministre Amadou Oury Bah, ainsi que les ministres en charge de l’Habitat et de l’Assainissement, sont déjà sur place aux côtés des services d’urgence. « On a beau demander à l’État guinéen, mais voilà aujourd’hui là où on est » Rachelle Bangoura, présidente des femmes de Dar-es-Salam, revient sur les alertes lancées par les habitants et les circonstances de l’éboulement. « on a beau demander à l’État guinéen, mais voilà aujourd’hui là où on est. Parce que même le vendredi, on était au palais avec des ministres qui sont chargés pour le décharge. Ils nous ont dit c’était aujourd’hui qu’ils allaient venir pour clôturer la décharge. Mais hier à 2h du matin, il y a des jeunes qui sont partis taper ma porte, soi-disant qu’il y a un éboulement.Maintenant, c’est en ce moment on est sorti. Parce que à un premier temps, il y avait une partie qui était tombée sur des gens. Maintenant, des gens qui étaient venus secourir des autres, c’est tombé maintenant pour une deuxième fois. Ça c’était vers les 3h. Mais le nombre de décès, on ne peut pas estimer ça d’abord, parce qu’on ne connaît pas encore. » Rencontré au pied de la montagne d’ordures, Mohamed Camara est toujours sans nouvelles de ses deux enfants. Ces derniers vivaient avec leur mère dans l’immeuble qui s’est affaissé. Très ému et en larmes, ce père de famille, domicilié à Dabondy, appelle à l’aide pour retrouver ses enfants, « même s’il ne s’agit que de leurs corps ». Pour l’heure, plusieurs cas de décès et plusieurs blessés sont signalés. Sur place, les parents des disparus restent partagés entre l’espoir de retrouver leurs proches et les larmes. Dans cette situation douloureuse, Mariama Ciré Kallo affirme avoir perdu cinq membres de sa famille.«j’ai perdu tous les membres de ma famille. Je sors très tôt le matin et rentre la nuit à cause de ces enfants ma raison de rester à Conakry est éteinte.Yaya kallo, M’mah kallo ,Issiaga kallo,Younoussa Kallo et Fanta Kallo» Mohamed Camara sans nouvelles de ses deux enfants Dans la même situation, Mohamed Camara n’a toujours pas retrouvé ses deux enfants, Mohamed et Souleymane, âgés respectivement de 12 et 16 ans. «mes enfants Mohamed et Souleymane sont dans le Bâtiment effondré. l’un a douze ans l’autre 16 , depuis cette date je n’ai aucune nouvelle d’eux. Peu importe s’ils sont morts ou vivants qu’ils m’aident à les avoir» Cette nouvelle catastrophe ravive le souvenir du précédent éboulement meurtrier survenu à Dar-es-Salam. Le 22 août 2017, une partie de la montagne d’ordures s’était effondrée, ensevelissant plusieurs habitations et causant la mort de plusieurs personnes. Huit ans après ce drame, les victimes avaient été commémorées à Dar-es-Salam en août 2025. Les familles et les habitants avaient notamment renouvelé leur appel aux autorités pour la sécurisation et la délocalisation de la décharge. Malgré les alertes répétées sur les risques liés à la saturation de la décharge, les populations riveraines sont restées exposées aux éboulements et autres dangers liés au site. La nouvelle tragédie survenue dans la nuit de samedi à dimanche vient ainsi raviver les inquiétudes des habitants de Dar-es-Salam, alors que les secours poursuivent leurs opérations pour tenter de retrouver les personnes encore portées disparues. Le bilan définitif de cet éboulement reste attendu. Mayi L’article Éboulement de Dar-es-Salam : plusieurs victimes ensevelies, des familles à la recherche de leurs proches est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Les pèlerins de justice et paix se sont recueillis à la basilique Saint-Pierre du Vatican
items.description: Les 350 pèlerins sénégalais sont bien arrivés à Rome.Après une messe d'ouverture présidée par Monseigneur Paul Abel Mamba, Évêque de Tamba, les fidèles se sont rendus à la mythique place Saint-Pierre de Rome avant de visiter la Basilique Saint-Pierre. Dans la foi et le recueillement, les pèlerins sénégalais ont visité la Basilique Saint-Pierre et les tombeaux des papes. Lors de cette visite guidée, la sépulture de Saint-Pierre, premier Pape de l'Église Catholique, a été prise d'assaut par les pèlerins de justice et de paix ainsi que des milliers d'autres fidèles venus des différents coins du globe. Les pèlerins sénégalais ont profité de la visite pour prier pour leurs familles et le pays.Cette journée à la Basilique Saint-Pierre a été clôturée par une Messe présidée par Monseigneur Augustin Simel Ndiaye, Évêque de Saint-Louis et président du Comité interdiocésain national pour les pèlerinages Catholiques (Cinpec). Abbé Paul Louis Edouard Sarr a, dans son homélie, rappelé aux pèlerins de justice et de paix leur mission de partager la bonne nouvelle dans leurs familles, leurs Communautés religieuses car selon lui, les pèlerins doivent être des bergers comme Jésus, qui, pour sauver le monde a donné sa vie. Marie Bernadette SENE (envoyée spéciale)

items.title: Road in Duki to be named after female doctor who survived acid attack: Balochistan CM Bugti
items.description: Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti announced on Sunday that a major road in the Duki district will be named after Dr Mahnoor Nasir, a doctor who suffered an acid attack in June, in honour of her “bravery, resilience and services as a medical professional”. Dr Nasir, a 29-year-old female doctor at Quetta’s Civil Hospital, was seriously injured in June when a hospital employee allegedly threw acid on her, suffering severe burn injuries to her face, chest, legs and other parts of her body. The attacker, later identified by police as Humayun Shah, was said to have been kil­led in an encounter after law enforcers tra­ced him as he attempted to flee on a bus. In a post on X, the chief minister lauded the “bravery, courage and sense of duty” displayed by Dr Nasir and said that a road in Duki had been renamed after her. He maintained that Dr Nasir’s determination was an “example for the daughters of Balochistan”. “Recognising the services of brave and duty-bound citizens and encouraging them is our responsibility,” he wrote on X. The notification which CM Bugti shared stated that as a “token to public recognition of Dr Mahnoor Nasir, of her bravery, resilience and services as a medical professional, it has been decided to rename ‘Haji Amanullah Masjid Road, adjacent to Damani Chowk, Duki’ as ‘Dr Mahnoor Nasar Road, Duki’, with immediate effect”. The attack had drawn widespread condemnation, including from doctors, government officials and the courts. Following the incident, doctors in Quetta went on strike , demanding a thorough investigation. Only days after the attack, in a landmark judgment, the Supreme Court ruled that “vitriolage” (acid attack) was an offence more heinous than homicide.

items.title: Gamou 2026 : Vaste opération de sécurisation à Thiès et Tivaouane
items.description: À quelques jours du Gamou 2026, la Police nationale renforce son dispositif sécuritaire dans les zones sensibles de Thiès et Tivaouane. Une vaste opération menée dans la nuit du 21 au 22 août a permis l’interpellation de 50 personnes et la saisie de plusieurs dizaines de pièces. Dans la nuit du 21 au 22 août 2026, de 22 heures à 5 heures du matin, le Service régional de la Sécurité publique a conduit une opération de sécurisation de grande envergure dans les villes de Thiès et Tivaouane. L’opération, dirigée par le Commissaire principal de police Sofiétou Mbaye, a mobilisé les personnels des différents commissariats, avec l’appui des éléments du Groupement mobile d’intervention (GMI) de Thiès et des brigades de recherches. Les forces de sécurité ont concentré leurs interventions sur les zones criminogènes et les axes stratégiques, avec pour objectif de renforcer la présence policière et de prévenir les actes de délinquance à l’approche du Gamou. À Thiès, 35 personnes ont été interpellées. Parmi elles, 31 l’ont été pour vérification d’identité, trois pour ivresse publique manifeste et une pour non-exécution d’une décision de justice. Les policiers ont également immobilisé cinq véhicules et neuf motos pour diverses infractions, tandis que 84 pièces ont été saisies. À Tivaouane, 15 personnes ont été interpellées. Onze l’ont été pour vérification d’identité, deux pour ivresse publique manifeste, une pour non-exécution d’une décision de justice et une autre pour vol. Trente-cinq pièces ont par ailleurs été saisies. À travers cette opération, la Police nationale entend renforcer la sécurité dans les deux localités, dissuader les éventuels délinquants et anticiper les risques liés à l’affluence attendue à Tivaouane pour le Gamou 2026. Le dispositif vise ainsi à permettre aux fidèles et aux visiteurs de rejoindre la cité religieuse dans les meilleures conditions de sécurité. A.N

items.title: Meko Bono 2026: Vice President pledges agricultural revival as Atebubu hosts grand homecoming
items.description: Vice President Prof Jane Naana Opoku Agyemang has delivered a strong assurance to the farming communities of the Bono East Region, pledging government commitment to minimising post-harvest losses and boosting agricultural productivity under the flagship Feed Ghana programme. She made the pledge on Saturday when she graced the grand climax of the Meko Bono Homecoming and Festival 2026 in Atebubu, where she was received with traditional pomp and pageantry. The Vice President, who was the special guest of honour, used the platform to connect directly with the predominantly agrarian population, acknowledging their struggles and outlining tangible interventions to improve their livelihoods. “We hear your concerns, and we are acting,” Prof. Opoku Agyemang told the cheering crowd. “Through the Feed Ghana initiative, we are not only minimising post-harvest losses but also improving general agricultural productivity to create more jobs and generate substantial wealth for our people.” Her address struck a chord with the thousands of farmers gathered, who have long grappled with the challenge of losing significant portions of their harvest to poor storage and logistical constraints. The Vice President’s assurance signals a renewed push by the government to make agriculture a more sustainable and profitable venture for the region’s backbone workforce. A celebration of heritage and unity Beyond the political messaging, the Vice President took time to underscore the cultural significance of the Meko Bono festival, which has grown into a vital platform for celebrating the rich Bono heritage, reconnecting the diaspora with their roots, and fostering partnerships for tourism, investment, and community development. She admonished the people to let the festival serve as a vessel for preserving history and tradition through togetherness. “Let this festival preserve the history and tradition of the Bono people through togetherness, thereby creating partnerships for development,” she added, drawing thunderous applause from the assembled chiefs, elders, and youth. Chiefs welcome Veep, rally for development Hosting the Vice President was HRM Ohempon Dr Yeboah Asiamah, the Atebubumanhene and Chairman of the Meko Bono Advisory Board, who welcomed her and the thousands of visitors with open arms. In his address, the Paramount Chief emphasised the festival’s growing relevance as more than a cultural showcase, but a strategic vehicle for sustainable community development. “The Meko Bono spirit is the thread that binds us across generations,” the Chief stated. “We must leverage this unity to attract investment and build a prosperous future for our children.” Adding his voice, Osagyefo Oseadeeyo Dr Nana Agyemang Badu II, President of the Bono Regional House of Chiefs, lauded the remarkable cohesion displayed by the Bono people, describing their togetherness as a shining example worthy of emulation across the nation. “The togetherness we see here today is not by chance; it is the result of shared values and mutual respect,” he remarked. “This is the kind of unity that builds nations, and I call on all Ghanaians to learn from the Bono example.” A spectacle of culture and colour The festival grounds in Atebubu came alive with breathtaking cultural displays that captivated the Vice President and all in attendance. The thunderous rhythms of Fontomfrom drums filled the air, while gracefully choreographed Adowa dancers mesmerised onlookers with their intricate footwork and vibrant regalia. From elders adorned in rich, hand-woven smocks to the energetic youth participating in traditional war dances, the event was a stunning reminder that Ghana’s cultural heritage remains a living, breathing force that unites generations. Looking ahead As the sun dipped below the horizon over Atebubu, it was clear that the Meko Bono Homecoming 2026 had achieved far more than a cultural reunion. With the Vice President’s agricultural assurances and the chiefs’ rallying calls for unity, the people of Atebubu left the festival grounds not just with memories of a spectacular celebration, but with renewed hope for a future built on the solid foundation of their illustrious heritage. The festival has once again proven that the Bono people are not merely preserving their past; they are actively shaping their future through participation, partnership, and unwavering togetherness.

items.title: Burkina Faso : Le plan ORSEC testé en simulation pour évaluer la réactivité face aux catastrophes
items.description: Pour mieux faire face aux urgences, le ministère en charge de l'Administration territoriale a mené un grand exercice de simulation, ce 22 août 2026. Organisée avec la Brigade nationale de sapeurs-pompiers (BNSP) et la Direction générale de la protection civile (DGPC), cette activité visait à tester l'efficacité des secours et à mesurer leur capacité de réaction en cas de catastrophe naturelle. Samedi 22 août 2026. Après 72 heures de pluies torrentielles, des inondations sont signalées de part et d'autre du territoire national. Selon l'Agence nationale de la météorologie (ANAM), le niveau des eaux pourrait encore augmenter et atteindre des proportions critiques. À Ouagadougou, les habitations environnantes sont inondées à la suite du débordement des barrages n°2 et n°3. L'on enregistre des victimes de noyade et les voies d'accès sont impraticables. La situation impose l'évacuation d'urgence de près de 200 habitants. La salle COVACOS©️Faso7 Un peu plus loin, le ruissellement des eaux de pluie a provoqué un incendie dans une usine de produits chimiques de la zone industrielle de Kossodo. Le site et ses environs sont envahis par un nuage de fumée toxique, nécessitant une évacuation immédiate du périmètre. Sur place, parmi les 103 ouvriers présents, 10 ont été intoxiqués, 30 blessés et 5 brûlés. L'ensemble des opérations est suivi depuis le Centre opérationnel de veille, d'alerte et de coordination des opérations de secours (COVACOS), logé au sein de la DGPC. La direction des opérations du jour a été confiée à Sibiri de Issa Ouédraogo, directeur de cabinet du ministère en charge de l'Administration territoriale. Il a à ses côtés le commandant des opérations de secours (COS), le colonel Daba Naon, commandant de la BNSP. Le site d'accueille des victimes©️Faso7 Le dispositif mobilise six (06) groupes opérationnels : secours et sauvetage, santé, entraide et réhabilitation, sécurité publique, transport, et forces armées. Tous sont réunis dans la salle du COVACOS pour piloter les interventions en temps réel. C'est ce scénario de crise qui a servi de cadre à la simulation du plan ORSEC (Organisation de la réponse de sécurité civile), le mécanisme d'urgence déclenché lors des catastrophes majeures. Sur le terrain, les équipes s'activent. Au niveau des barrages n°2 et n°3, une embarcation se charge de transporter les victimes vers l'autre rive. Sur les berges, les sapeurs-pompiers accueillent et secourent progressivement les rescapés à leur descente du bateau. En bout de chaîne, les équipes médicales de la Croix-Rouge, du SAMU et de la BNSP prennent le relais. Une à une, les victimes sont examinées puis acheminées vers un site d'accueil, où le Secrétariat permanent du Conseil national de secours d'urgence et de réhabilitation (SP-CONASUR) assure leur prise en charge globale. L'étape de décontamination©️Faso7 À l'usine de Kossodo, la même chaîne de secours est déployée, mais sous de fortes contraintes sanitaires. Après l'explosion, les victimes sont d'abord secourues et mises à l'abri. Vient ensuite l'étape clé de la décontamination des blessés avant tout accès au poste médical avancé. Après examen par les unités de soins, les patients sont évacués à tour de rôle par les ambulances de la Croix-Rouge, du SAMU et de la BNSP. À l'issue des opérations, le bilan dressé par le capitaine Jean-Charles Tampanga, directeur de la réglementation et de la prévention à la DGPC, fait état de 167 victimes, dont un décès, 6 urgences absolues, 60 urgences relatives et 100 personnes impliquées. Il a souligné que l'opération a été un succès pour une première mise en œuvre, alors que l'arrêté portant sur le plan ORSEC n’avait pas été testé depuis 2012. Le directeur des opérations, Sibiri de Issa Ouédraogo, a rappelé que les équipes doivent rester en alerte, car « la catastrophe ne prévient pas ». Pour lui, cette simulation constitue une grande avancée dans l'acquisition de connaissances et le renforcement des capacités des acteurs. Elle rassure sur la capacité du Burkina Faso à faire face à de telles situations, d'autant plus que le plan ORSEC n'avait encore jamais fait l'objet d'un test depuis son adoption en 2012. L’article Burkina Faso : Le plan ORSEC testé en simulation pour évaluer la réactivité face aux catastrophes est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Russian skydiver Sergey Boytcov sets world record with 11,551-metre stratosphere jump
items.description: Russian skydiver Sergey Boytcov has set a world record after completing a jump from a hot-air balloon at an altitude of 11,551 metres in support of the 2026 International Festival of Youth. The record-breaking jump, undertaken ahead of Russia’s National Flag Day, surpassed the previous mark of 10,060 metres set by Polish extreme athletes. Boytcov, a multiple Russian and world record holder, completed the feat under the Stratum Jump 11–12 project, an initiative by Russian company Created by the Heavens aimed at reaching an altitude above 11,000 metres. During the jump, his free-fall speed exceeded 500 kilometres per hour, with the entire descent lasting seven minutes and 19 seconds. His parachute was successfully deployed at an altitude of 1,565 metres before he landed safely in the Ust-Kalmanka District of Russia’s Altai Territory. The hot-air balloon was piloted by Ivan Menyaylo, President of the Balloon Federation of Russia and a world champion, with flight engineer Denis Efremov also on board. The balloon remained airborne for more than three hours before the crew landed safely. The balloon itself reached a maximum altitude of 11,610 metres, setting a new Russian national record and surpassing the previous mark of 10,678 metres established in 2025 by Russian explorer Fyodor Konyukhov and Menyaylo in the same region. Boytcov, who celebrated his birthday on August 15, described the achievement as the most memorable experience of his life. “We achieved something that not long ago seemed impossible,” he said. He attributed the feat to the collective efforts of engineers, pilots and other members of the project team, adding that he was particularly proud that the record was achieved in Russia using domestically manufactured equipment. Boytcov dedicated the achievement to his country ahead of National Flag Day and to the International Festival of Youth – 2026. “I hope our example shows young people all over the world that even the boldest goals become reality when they are backed by knowledge, hard work, a team, and belief in the outcome,” he said. Preparations for the attempt involved navigating extreme conditions at more than 11 kilometres above the ground, where temperatures dropped to minus 59 degrees Celsius. With support from Russia’s Roscosmos State Corporation, Boytcov underwent a test ascent in a pressure chamber at the Cosmonaut Training Centre, simulating conditions at an altitude of 12 kilometres. Equipment was also tested at temperatures as low as minus 60 degrees Celsius, while the athlete rehearsed aspects of the jump in a wind tunnel. Boytcov, from Klin in the Moscow Region, has more than 25 years of experience in the sport and has completed over 2,000 jumps. He is also chief executive of Created by the Heavens and holds a USPA Category D licence. The project received support from several Russian institutions, including the Ministry of Sport, Russian Olympic Committee, State Duma Committee on Physical Culture and Sport, Roscosmos and the Federal Air Transport Agency. The record attempt was held in support of the International Festival of Youth, scheduled to take place in Ekaterinburg from September 11 to 17, 2026. The festival, being organised under Russia’s Youth and Children national project, is expected to bring together 10,000 young leaders from 191 countries. Organisers say participants will comprise 5,000 Russians and 5,000 foreign nationals, including 1,000 teenagers aged between 14 and 17. Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree establishing the international youth event on December 29, 2025. The 2026 festival will be held under the theme, “Follow Your Dream”.
